title: Concert Ticket Drop
summary: 30,000 fans hit refresh at 10:00. Every write is a race for the same seats, and the latency budget is razor-thin.
scenario: A stadium tour goes on sale. 30,000 requests per second: 70% checking availability, 30% trying to buy. 90% of those buys fight over the same front sections.
The current stack is undersized, has no locking (so it oversells), and puts every purchase on a single SQL primary.
Build a design that doesn't oversell, doesn't drop fans, and keeps average latency at 47 ms or less. Pick your coordination service carefully, because they aren't equally fast.

nonFunctional: 90% of purchases fight over the same sections
Average latency at or below 47 ms

objectives.label: No unsafe contended writes (no double bookings)
Average latency at or below 47 ms

hints: Work through it in order: capacity first (which components are red?), then correctness (Unsafe writes), then latency.
9,000 writes per second can't go to one SQL primary. Use NoSQL with enough shards (4 replicas). Scale the API to about 30 replicas so it runs under 70%.
Add a lock service for the 8,100 contended writes/s. ZooKeeper adds about 6 ms to each and misses the latency target. A Redis Lock with 2 replicas (about 2 ms) fits. Use 3 LB replicas too.
explanation: Correctness, capacity and latency pull against each other. Locks add a hop to every contended write, so at high volume the lock's own latency becomes a design constraint.
Redis locks are the pragmatic choice for short, high-volume critical sections like seat holds. Back them with a database uniqueness constraint so that a lock lost to a GC pause can never oversell.
ZooKeeper gives stronger guarantees (sessions, ordering, no clock assumptions) and is better for leader election and long-held locks, but every acquire is a quorum write.
Real ticketing systems go further: a virtual waiting room in front, rate limiting per user, and short seat holds (reserve for 5 minutes, then confirm payment) to cut contention.
